title: Conjugates of any Borel cover a connected affine algebraic group
statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure] and let $G$ be a smooth connected affine group scheme of finite type over $k$ [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Subgroups mean closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. A Borel subgroup is a maximal smooth connected solvable subgroup, where solvable means that successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups eventually become trivial. Borel subgroups of $G$ exist. For every Borel subgroup $B\subseteq G$, the map on rational points
$$G(k)\times B(k)\longrightarrow G(k),\qquad (g,b)\longmapsto gbg^{-1}$$
is surjective. Thus every element of $G(k)$ is conjugate to an element of any prescribed Borel subgroup. No reductivity hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Definition 17.6 and following sentence, printed pp.353–354 (existence); Theorem 17.33(b) and its proof, and Corollary 17.34, printed p.362 (conjugation covering).

proof.text: The trivial subgroup is smooth, connected and solvable. Among smooth connected solvable subgroups containing it choose one of largest dimension: dimensions are bounded integers, and a strict inclusion of smooth connected subgroups strictly increases dimension, by [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products]. It is therefore maximal under inclusion, so is a Borel. The same argument shows that every given smooth connected solvable subgroup is contained in a Borel.

source.place: Definition 17.6 and sentence immediately following it, pp.353--354

proof.text: Fix any prescribed Borel $B$. By [lem-sfb-borel-maximal-torus-conjugacy], choose a torus $T\subseteq B$ maximal in $G$. Apply [lem-sfb-neutral-torus-centralizer-cartan-structure] to obtain the smooth connected solvable subgroup $C=C_G(T)^\circ$, containing $T$, its product structure, and the finite set $N/C(k)$ of normalizing cosets.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 17.33(b), p.362; Proposition 17.28, p.360

proof.text: By step 1 extend $C$ to a Borel $B'$. Both $B'$ and $B$ contain the maximal torus $T$. By [lem-sfb-torus-normalizer-borel-transitivity] choose $n\in G(k)$ normalizing $T$ and satisfying $nB'n^{-1}=B$. Conjugation by $n$ preserves the centralizer functor of $T$ and its identity component $C$; hence $C=nCn^{-1}\subseteq nB'n^{-1}=B$. This proves the containment needed here without using connectedness of the full centralizer.

Choose the semisimple $t\in T(k)$ of [lem-sfb-torus-regular-semisimple-element], so that $C_G(t)=C_G(T)$ on all algebras. Form $G/C$ using [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry]; every rational point is a coset $xC$ with $x\in G(k)$. If $txC=xC$, then $x^{-1}tx\in C(k)$. It is semisimple, because applying a representation conjugates the diagonalizable matrix representing $t$. By the structure statement in step 2 it lies in $T(k)$. Consequently $xTx^{-1}$ centralizes $t$ on every algebra: conjugating the commutation of $T$ with $x^{-1}tx$ proves this directly. Equality of centralizer functors puts $xTx^{-1}$ inside $C_G(T)$. Since this torus is connected and contains the identity, it lies in the open identity component $C$. Every torus in $C$ lies in $T$ by the structure statement, so $xTx^{-1}\subseteq T$. Maximality of $xTx^{-1}$ as a torus of $G$ implies equality. Therefore $x$ normalizes $T$, hence also its centralizer and its identity component $C$. The fixed cosets thus inject into the finite set $N/C(k)$ of step 2, by the map sending $xC$ to the same right coset. Its injectivity is exactly equality of right cosets. The fixed-point set of $t$ on $(G/C)(k)$ is finite.

Apply the finite-fixed-coset clause of [lem-sfb-subgroup-conjugation-incidence-criterion] with $H=C$ and $h_0=t$. All groups are smooth and connected, and step 4 supplies its finiteness hypothesis. There is a nonempty open $V\subseteq G$ with $V(k)\subseteq S_C$. Since step 3 gives $C\subseteq B$, each expression $gcg^{-1}$ with $c\in C(k)$ is also of the form $gbg^{-1}$ with $b\in B(k)$. Thus $V(k)\subseteq S_B$.

Form the quotient $G/B$ by [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry]. Its quotient projection meets the hypotheses of [lem-sfb-borel-quotient-proper-geometry], which gives properness of $G/B$ and integrality of $G$. Apply the proper-quotient clause of [lem-sfb-subgroup-conjugation-incidence-criterion] with $H=B$ to obtain a closed subset $Z\subseteq |G|$ such that $Z(k)=S_B$. Suppose $Z\ne |G|$. Integrality makes $G$ irreducible, so the nonempty open $V$ of step 5 meets the nonempty open $G\setminus Z$. This intersection has a closed point of $G$, since closed points are dense by [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space]. Its residue field is $k$ by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base], so it gives a rational point in $V(k)$ outside $Z(k)$, contrary to step 5. Hence $Z=|G|$ and $S_B=G(k)$. Unpacking $S_B$ gives, for every $a\in G(k)$, elements $g\in G(k)$ and $b\in B(k)$ with $a=gbg^{-1}$, exactly the required surjectivity.
